plain_definition: A contract that pays for covered repairs after the factory warranty, for a set number of months and miles.
example: A 60-month, 75,000-mile contract that pays for an engine repair.

plain_definition: Pays the difference between what a car is worth and what is still owed on the loan if the car is totaled or stolen.
example: The car is worth $18,000, the loan is $22,000: GAP pays the $4,000 gap.

plain_definition: Smaller add-on products sold in the finance office, such as tire and wheel, key replacement or dent repair.
example: A tire-and-wheel plan sold with a used car.

plain_definition: Written is the money booked when a contract is sold. Earned is the part used up as coverage time passes.
example: A $1,200, 36-month contract is $1,200 written on day one and about $400 earned after a year.

plain_definition: The part of the premium that has been used up by coverage time so far.
example: After 6 of 24 months, about a quarter of the premium is earned.

plain_definition: Claims divided by the money set aside to pay them. Over 100% means claims cost more than was set aside.
example: $70 of claims on $100 of earned claims reserve is a 70% loss ratio.

plain_definition: Claims plus selling costs plus the admin fee, divided by earned premium. Over 100% means the book lost money.
example: $95 of all costs on $100 earned is 95%: a small profit.

plain_definition: Handing part of the risk, and the reserve that pays for it, to a reinsurance company, often one a dealer owns.
example: A dealer's own reinsurance company takes the claims risk on the contracts that dealer sells.

plain_definition: A company that takes on part of the claims risk in return for the matching reserve; dealers often own one.
example: A dealer group sets up its own reinsurance company to share in the profit on its contracts.

plain_definition: A way for a dealer to share in the risk and profit of its own contracts, through a company it owns.
example: A dealer-owned company receives a distribution when its loss ratio stays low.

plain_definition: Money held in reserve to pay future claims, instead of backing the contracts with an insurance policy.
example: A state requires the provider to hold reserve equal to a share of what it collected.

plain_definition: The part of each contract's dealer cost set aside to pay claims. Loss ratios on this site use it as the bottom half.
example: Of a $1,000 dealer cost, $600 might go to the claims reserve.

plain_definition: An insurance policy that stands behind the obligor, so claims are paid even if the obligor cannot pay.
example: If the obligor fails, the CLIP insurer pays covered claims.

plain_definition: Money for claims that have already happened but have not been reported yet.
example: A car broke down last week but the shop has not called in the claim.

plain_definition: What a group of contracts is expected to cost in claims once every claim is in.
example: Reported losses plus IBNR plus claims still to come on active contracts.

plain_definition: Premium collected for coverage time that has not happened yet.
example: Halfway through a contract, about half the premium is still unearned.

plain_definition: A way to split premium over a contract term that counts the early months more heavily than a straight line.
example: Used for some cancel refunds; the reverse form earns slowly, to match claims that come late.

plain_definition: The rule that says how fast premium counts as earned over the contract term.
example: Straight-line earns the same each month; a slow curve earns more near the end.

plain_definition: The dealer sending the money for the contracts it sold to the administrator.
example: A dealer remits $12,000 for last week's contracts; 30 days or more after entry is late.

plain_definition: A fee billed to a dealer that remits late, as a set share of the late amount.
example: A $10,000 late remittance at 1.5% is a $150 late fee.

plain_definition: Money taken back from a dealer or agent when a contract cancels, for the part not yet earned.
example: A contract cancels after 6 months; the dealer gives back its share of the unearned part.

plain_definition: The company legally on the hook to pay claims on a contract.
example: The provider is the obligor; a CLIP insurer stands behind it.

plain_definition: The producer sells the contract (the dealer or agent). The provider issues it and is often the obligor.
example: A dealer is the producer; the warranty company is the provider.

plain_definition: A contract that is active today: sold, paid for and not yet expired or cancelled.
example: A 48-month contract sold two years ago and never cancelled is in force.

plain_definition: A contract that was sold but is not finished: paperwork or payment is still missing.
example: The co-buyer has not signed yet, so the contract cannot become active.

plain_definition: The share of contracts that were cancelled. By sale group, it follows contracts sold together over time.
example: Of 1,000 contracts sold in a quarter, 150 cancelled so far: 15%.

plain_definition: A cancelled contract that is turned back on.
example: A customer cancels by mistake and the contract is reinstated a week later.

plain_definition: What the dealer owes the administrator for a contract, before the dealer adds its markup.
example: The customer pays $2,000, the dealer cost is $1,200, the markup is $800.

plain_definition: Retail price minus dealer cost: what the store keeps.
example: Retail $2,000 minus dealer cost $1,200 is an $800 markup.

plain_definition: The administrator's fee for running the contracts and handling claims.
example: A set dollar amount out of each contract's dealer cost.

plain_definition: Commission, insurer fee and premium tax: what it costs to sell a contract.
example: Agent commission plus the insurer fee plus state premium tax.

plain_definition: The part of the underwriting profit paid back to a dealer that shares in the risk.
example: A dealer-owned company with low claims receives a yearly distribution.

plain_definition: Old enough to judge: a dealer-owned company must run a set time before any distribution.
example: No distribution in the first years, because claims come late.

plain_definition: Commission paid to an agent before it is earned; it is worked off as the contracts earn.
example: An agent gets $5,000 up front and earns it back over the contract terms.

plain_definition: Money held for one open claim until it is paid.
example: A shop quotes $3,000 for a repair; $3,000 is held until payment.

plain_definition: Claims paid plus money held for open claims.
example: $50,000 paid plus $10,000 held is $60,000 incurred.

plain_definition: How many claims each contract makes per year of coverage.
example: 300 claims on 1,000 contract-years is 0.3 claims a year.

plain_definition: The average amount paid on a paid claim.
example: $600,000 paid on 500 paid claims is $1,200 per claim.

plain_definition: A claim not paid because the repair was not covered by the contract.
example: A worn-out part the contract excludes.

plain_definition: A claim soon after the contract starts, which can mean a problem existed at sale.
example: A transmission claim 20 days after the contract began.

plain_definition: The part of a repair the customer pays before the contract pays the rest.
example: A $100 deductible on a $900 repair: the contract pays $800.

plain_definition: An extra charge for a vehicle trait that raises risk, such as diesel, four-wheel drive or commercial use.
example: A commercial-use truck carries a surcharge on its contract.

plain_definition: The price list: dealer cost by term, miles, vehicle class and coverage level.
example: 36 months, 36,000 miles, class 2, top coverage: one price.

plain_definition: The 17-character number that identifies one vehicle.
example: Shown masked on this site so it cannot be traced.

plain_definition: A motorhome or camper. It has two vehicle numbers: the coach and the chassis it is built on.
example: A motorhome built on a truck chassis.

plain_definition: The vehicle number of the truck frame an RV is built on; claims on the engine need it.
example: The coach has one number and the chassis has another.

plain_definition: The code of the approved contract form a contract was sold on.
example: A state checks every contract was sold on a form it approved.

plain_definition: A second buyer on the vehicle loan; one old source column labelled lienholder actually holds the co-buyer.
example: A spouse who co-signed the loan.

plain_definition: A partner program that sells under its own brand; each sees only its own dealers.
example: Three partner programs share the platform, each walled off.

plain_definition: A set of reports filtered to one dealer, so it never sees another dealer's numbers.
example: Production, pending contracts and payments for one store.

plain_definition: The last 12 complete months added together.
example: In November, T12 covers last November through this October.

plain_definition: Everything since the start of the program.
example: All contracts ever sold, up to today.

plain_definition: From January 1 to today.
example: In May, YTD covers January to May.

plain_definition: The month a transaction is booked in the ledger. Closed months are never changed.
example: A late claim payment is booked in the first open month.

plain_definition: The month the car broke down, used for claim trends.
example: A breakdown in March reported in May counts in March.

plain_definition: Contracts sold in the same period, followed together over time.
example: Everything sold in the first quarter of a year.

plain_definition: One contract active for one year; the fair way to compare claim counts.
example: Two contracts active six months each make one contract-year.

plain_definition: An automatic check that stops reports publishing when the data looks wrong.
example: If claims stop matching contracts, nothing new is published.

plain_definition: Proving counts and dollars match from the source system to the reports.
example: 20,000 contracts in the source, 20,000 in the reports.

plain_definition: A promise about service, such as reports ready before 7 in the morning.
example: Reports ready by 7 on 19 of 20 business days is 95%.

plain_definition: A company that sells no new contracts but still pays claims on the old ones until they end.
example: A dealer-owned company closed to new business last year.
